title: Research Journal #34 — What Makes a Scientific Record Trustworthy?
html:
Imagine two scientists investigating the same physical phenomenon.

They use the same equations, the same numerical parameters, and the same software. Their investigations produce files containing exactly the same bytes.

Have they independently reproduced the same scientific result?

Not necessarily. Identical outputs may be consistent with independent reproduction, but they do not establish it. Independence depends on the actual methods, execution histories, dependencies, and conditions of the investigations.

Identical files do not tell us whether the investigations were actually independent, whether the software ran twice, whether the same data was reused, or whether both researchers relied on an incorrect assumption.

Now consider a different situation.

A scientist revisits an earlier calculation, discovers an error, and produces a corrected result.

Should the corrected result replace the original record?

Or should both be preserved, together with the relationship explaining what changed and why?

These questions go to the heart of scientific reproducibility.

They also became central to the next stage of Beyond the Light Barrier's scientific research framework.

Following the November 2 conceptual freeze of ARCH-003, the Next Architecture Exploration program (NAE-1) began making more specific detailed-design decisions.

Two decisions were recorded on November 2 and November 3.

They concerned the structure of research records and the meaning of their identities.

Neither decision implemented new software.

But together they established important conceptual foundations for how the framework should preserve scientific history.

From Architecture to Detailed Design

Research Journal #33 described the acceptance and conceptual freeze of ARCH-003—Independent Scientific Records with Claim-Scoped Federation.

The freeze established four shared architectural responsibilities:

  • Research Record and Graph
  • Artifact and Integrity
  • Execution and Lifecycle
  • Discovery and Resolution

It also established six governing invariants, including historical truth, scientific authority, evidence scope, and epistemic conservatism.

Those principles provided a controlled conceptual baseline.

But they did not yet determine every detail of how scientific records should be represented.

For example, what should the framework consider a record?

Should scientific claims be handled separately from other kinds of research information?

How should relationships among records be represented?

And when two records look alike, what determines whether they are actually the same record?

These questions became the subjects of the first two adopted detailed-design decisions.

DD-001 — Research Graph: Records and Relationships

On November 2, NAE-1 adopted detailed-design decision DD-001.

Its central organizing principle was:

Research Graph = Records + Relationships

A graph, in this context, is a structure consisting of identifiable objects and the relationships connecting them.

The objects are research records.

The relationships describe how those records are connected.

Consider a hypothetical investigation into a proposed gravitational effect.

The investigation might produce:

  • An analytic derivation based on a particular physical model
  • A numerical simulation using specified equations and boundary conditions
  • A dataset containing the simulation output
  • A comparison between the analytic and numerical results
  • A scientific assertion interpreting what the comparison establishes
  • A later correction or independent reproduction attempt

These activities are related, but they are not interchangeable.

A derivation is not a simulation.

A simulation output is not automatically a scientific conclusion.

And an assertion about a result is not the same thing as the evidence offered to support it.

A research graph provides a conceptual way to preserve those distinctions while recording justified relationships among the records.

For example, a scientific assertion might reference a simulation result as supporting evidence.

But the existence of that relationship does not, by itself, establish that the assertion is scientifically valid.

The relationship records a connection that must still be interpreted according to the relevant scientific context.

This is consistent with one of ARCH-003's central principles: shared infrastructure should preserve and coordinate scientific information without silently becoming the authority that decides what the information means.

Why Assertions Matter

DD-001 also adopted an important distinction.

An Assertion is a scientifically distinct, specialized kind of Record.

An assertion expresses something being claimed or interpreted.

That makes it different from simply preserving an artifact or recording that an operation occurred.

Suppose a simulation produces a numerical value.

The framework might preserve the simulation's inputs, execution details, output, and relevant artifacts.

A researcher might then assert that the result supports a particular physical interpretation.

That assertion must remain distinguishable from the underlying simulation record.

Why?

Because the simulation may have executed correctly while the scientific interpretation remains unsupported.

Or the interpretation may depend on assumptions that later prove incorrect.

A subsequent investigation might challenge the assertion without changing the historical fact that the simulation occurred.

Treating assertions as scientifically distinct records creates a conceptual basis for preserving those differences.

It does not automatically determine whether any particular assertion is true.

DD-002 — What Gives a Record Its Identity?

On November 3, NAE-1 adopted DD-002.

This decision addressed durable identity and relational lineage in scientific records.

The central issue was that scientific identity cannot be reduced to a single convenient technical property.

Consider two files with identical contents.

A computer can calculate a cryptographic hash of each file.

If the files contain exactly the same bytes, the same hashing algorithm will produce the same hash.

That can be useful for checking content equality and integrity.

But it does not tell us everything about the scientific circumstances in which the files were produced.

One file might be the output of a new computation.

Another might be a copy of an earlier result.

A third might have been independently generated using the same inputs and algorithm.

The files could be byte-for-byte identical while representing different research histories.

Identical content does not necessarily imply identical scientific identity.

DD-002 therefore adopted a context-sensitive approach to durable record identity and relational lineage.

The conceptual distinction matters because a record's identity may depend on its role and context within an investigation, not merely on its stored bytes.

Identity Is Not Validity

Another important distinction is that identifying a record does not establish whether the record is scientifically correct.

A durable identifier helps us refer to a particular research record consistently.

It does not prove that the associated calculation is accurate.

It does not establish that an experiment was properly calibrated.

And it does not demonstrate that a scientific interpretation is justified.

These are separate questions requiring appropriate evidence.

Identity Is Not Independence

A record can have a distinct identity without representing an independent scientific reproduction.

Imagine that two researchers create separate records describing the same simulation output.

If both records ultimately depend on the same execution, they are not evidence of two independent executions.

Similarly, copying a dataset into another research record does not create an independent experimental measurement.

Independence must be established through the actual history, methods, dependencies, and conditions of the investigations.

It cannot be inferred merely from the existence of separate record identifiers.

Identity Is Not Performance

A record's identity also does not establish that the operation associated with it completed successfully.

A preserved record might document a failed calculation, an interrupted execution, or an inconclusive investigation.

Those outcomes still matter.

A trustworthy scientific framework should be designed to preserve these outcomes without treating the existence of a record as evidence of successful completion. Whether the eventual implementation satisfies that requirement remains to be verified.

This is especially relevant to our earlier AR-1.7 work, where preserving incomplete operations, failure observations, and unresolved findings was essential to maintaining an accurate research history.

Why Relationships and Lineage Matter

Scientific records rarely exist in isolation.

A later investigation may depend on an earlier calculation.

A simulation may use a particular software version.

A scientific assertion may cite multiple pieces of evidence.

A corrected result may supersede an earlier interpretation.

An independent reproduction attempt may seek to evaluate a previous finding.

These relationships form part of the scientific history.

But they must be explicit enough to avoid creating misleading conclusions.

For example, a relationship indicating that one record references another does not automatically mean that the first record validates the second.

Likewise, a relationship indicating that a result was reproduced must be supported by evidence appropriate to the claimed reproduction.

The graph provides a structure for recording relationships.

The scientific context determines what those relationships actually establish.

This distinction helps preserve the boundary between managing research information and evaluating scientific evidence.

What About Cryptographic Hashes?

Cryptographic hashes are useful tools for preserving artifact integrity.

They can help determine whether stored bytes match a previously recorded value.

But their role has limits.

Matching cryptographic hashes can provide strong evidence of byte-level agreement when the same suitable algorithm is used and the hashes, source artifacts, and comparison process are trustworthy. Hash agreement alone does not establish scientific correctness, independent execution, or provenance.

It is not evidence that the scientific contents are correct.

It does not prove that two computations were independently performed.

And it does not establish that two artifacts with identical contents have the same scientific provenance.

For Beyond the Light Barrier, this distinction is important.

We may eventually need to preserve analytic calculations, simulation outputs, experimental datasets, source code, research interpretations, and reproductions across different computing environments.

Content integrity is one part of that challenge.

Scientific identity and evidentiary meaning are separate parts.

DD-002 preserves that separation at the conceptual design level.

Why This Matters for Beyond the Light Barrier

Our research explores questions involving advanced communication, propulsion, spacetime, and other potentially unconventional physical mechanisms.

Some investigations involve established mathematical theory.

Others examine speculative models or project hypotheses.

Some may produce numerical results.

Others may eventually lead to physical experiments.

A research framework must not blur these categories.

Suppose a proposed spacetime model produces an interesting numerical result.

We need to preserve the equations, assumptions, parameters, numerical method, and output.

We also need to distinguish the result from any scientific assertion made about it.

If another investigation repeats the computation, we need enough history to determine what was actually repeated and whether the repetition provides independent evidence.

If a later analysis identifies an error, we need to preserve both the original record and the correction.

And if the model ultimately fails, that failure may still constrain future research.

A trustworthy research system should make it possible to reconstruct that history without rewriting inconvenient results or confusing records with conclusions.

DD-001 and DD-002 provide conceptual design decisions intended to support those goals.

They do not demonstrate that the resulting software will successfully achieve them.

What the Decisions Did Not Establish

The November 2 and November 3 decisions were adopted detailed-design decisions within the frozen ARCH-003 conceptual architecture.

They did not select concrete database technologies.

They did not establish final storage schemas or application programming interfaces.

They did not specify deployment infrastructure.

They did not authorize implementation.

And they did not demonstrate that an implemented research graph could meet the project's performance, durability, usability, or scientific integrity requirements.

The eight inherited AR-1.7 architectural findings also remained open.

No corrective implementation or verification of those findings was established by these decisions.

Likewise, no physical experiment, independent scientific reproduction, or faster-than-light phenomenon was demonstrated.

These decisions concern the conceptual organization of scientific information—not a new result in physics.

What Comes Next?

The adopted decisions establish a foundation for further detailed design.

But important questions remain.

How should records and relationships be represented in actual software?

How should the framework preserve identity and lineage when investigations evolve?

How should it distinguish a recovery operation from a genuinely independent rerun?

How should it handle incomplete work, conflicting evidence, corrections, and superseded scientific assertions?

And how can these responsibilities be implemented without creating unnecessary complexity?

Those questions require additional design work and, eventually, implementation and verification.

The conceptual decisions provide direction.

Their practical adequacy remains to be established.

Research Reflection

Scientific trust does not come from the mere existence of a record.

It comes from the evidence, methods, provenance, and reasoning that allow the record's significance to be evaluated.

A hash can help establish that bytes have not changed.

An identifier can help establish which record we are discussing.

A relationship can help describe how records are connected.

But none of those mechanisms, by itself, establishes that a scientific conclusion is true.

That requires scientific reasoning and evidence appropriate to the claim.

For Beyond the Light Barrier, this is a foundational distinction.

We want to preserve research history accurately enough that future investigators can understand what was attempted, what succeeded, what failed, what remains uncertain, and what evidence supports each conclusion.

A trustworthy scientific record must preserve the difference between what exists, what happened, what is claimed, and what has actually been established.

The November 2–3 decisions do not complete that task.

They establish two documented conceptual steps toward it.
